lead: Detailing turns the calculated steel into bars a site team can cut, bend, place and concrete: each bar's diameter, position, length, shape and anchorage, drawn and listed in a bar bending schedule. The code's detailing rules on cover, spacing, minimum and maximum steel, stirrup hooks and side-face bars exist because a correct design with poor detailing still cracks, corrodes or fails at a joint. Some syllabi call this 'design requirements as per the current code' or 'detailing requirements'.
prereq: You need: development length, laps and curtailment from Bond, anchorage and development length and Lap splices and curtailment of bars.

blocks.text: Nominal cover is the design depth of concrete over all steel, including the stirrups, written on the drawing. It protects the steel from corrosion and fire and gives the bars room to bond. IS 456 sets it by exposure: 20 mm mild, 30 mm moderate, 45 mm severe, 50 mm very severe, 75 mm extreme (for mild exposure it may be 5 mm less for main bars up to 12 mm). Fire resistance may need more. Longitudinal bars in columns need at least 40 mm, and not less than the bar diameter.

Because the nominal cover is measured to the stirrup, the main bar sits deeper: its cover is the nominal cover plus the stirrup diameter. Effective depth d is measured to the centroid of the main bars: d = D − cover − stirrup diameter − φ/2 for one layer.

sections.h3: Bar spacing and amount of steel

items: Horizontal clear distance between bars: at least the diameter of the larger bar and the nominal maximum aggregate size plus 5 mm (25 mm for 20 mm aggregate).
Two or more layers: bars vertically in line, with a vertical clear gap of at least 15 mm, two thirds of the maximum aggregate size and the largest bar diameter.
Maximum clear distance between tension bars in beams, for crack control: 180 mm for Fe415 and 150 mm for Fe500 when no moment is redistributed.
Tension steel: at least 0.85 b d/f<sub>y</sub> and not more than 0.04 b D. Compression steel: not more than 0.04 b D, held by stirrups.
Side-face bars: 0.1 % of the web area, shared between the two faces at 300 mm or less, when the web is deeper than 750 mm; in beams under torsion when a dimension exceeds 450 mm.

blocks.where: s is the clear spacing between n bars of diameter φ in one layer (mm); b is the beam width (mm); c is the nominal cover (mm); φ<sub>s</sub> is the stirrup diameter (mm).

sections.h3: Stirrups, hooks and the bar bending schedule

blocks.text: A stirrup is anchored when its end is bent at least 90° round a bar of at least its own diameter and continued 8φ, or bent 135° and continued 6φ, or bent 180° and continued 4φ. Torsion stirrups and stirrups in earthquake zones use the 135° hook, so they cannot open when the cover spalls. Bars are bent round a mandrel to the bend radii of the bending code and SP 34, the handbook on concrete reinforcement and detailing; a bend that is too tight crushes the concrete inside it and can crack the bar.

items: Draw the section to scale: outline, cover, stirrup, main bars; check clear spacing.
Draw the elevation: bar marks, cut-off points, laps and their lengths, anchorage at the supports.
Mark the stirrup zones: '10 φ @ 140 c/c', where φ is the bar diameter and c/c means centre to centre, with the first stirrup 50 mm from the face.
Write the bar bending schedule: bar mark, diameter, shape, number, cutting length and weight. Weight per metre = φ²/162 kg/m with φ in mm.

blocks.text: The schedule and the drawing must agree bar for bar; the fabricator works only from the schedule. Show every lap and anchorage as a dimension, never as a note 'lap as required'.

examples.question: Detail the section of the edge beam designed for combined bending, shear and torsion: b = 300 mm, D = 600 mm, four 20 mm bottom bars, two 12 mm top bars, one 12 mm bar on each side face, 10 mm closed stirrups at 140 mm, moderate exposure, 20 mm aggregate. Check the cover, the clear spacing of the bottom bars, the effective depth and the side-face spacing.
steps: Moderate exposure: nominal cover 30 mm to the stirrups. Cover to the main bars = 30 + 10 = 40 mm.
Clear spacing of the four 20 mm bars: (220 − 4 × 20)/3 = 140/3 = 46.7 mm.
Minimum: greater of φ = 20 mm and 20 + 5 = 25 mm, so 25 mm. Maximum for Fe415: 180 mm. 46.7 mm lies between, so one layer works.
Effective depth: d = 600 − 30 − 10 − 20/2 = 550 mm, as assumed in the design.
Side faces: top bar centre 46 mm and bottom bar centre 50 mm from the faces; a side bar at mid-depth (300 mm) leaves gaps of 254 mm and 250 mm, below 300 mm.
examples.answer: Cover 30 mm to the stirrups (40 mm to the main bars); clear spacing 46.7 mm (between 25 and 180 mm); d = 550 mm; steel 1257 mm² within 338 to 7200 mm²; side-face gaps 254 and 250 mm. The section is properly detailed.

examples.question: Write the weight lines of the bar bending schedule for the same beam over a 6.0 m clear span on 300 mm supports: four 20 mm bottom bars and two 12 mm top bars each 6.54 m long, and 10 mm stirrups at 140 mm with a cutting length of 1.72 m.
steps: Number of stirrups: first and last 50 mm from the faces, so (6000 − 100)/140 + 1 = 43.1, round up to 44.
Stirrup cutting length: centreline 230 mm × 530 mm gives 2 × (230 + 530) = 1520 mm, plus 100 mm for each 135° hook (a common site allowance) = 1720 mm. Weight: 44 × 1.72 × 0.617 = 46.7 kg.
examples.answer: Bottom bars 64.6 kg, top bars 11.6 kg, 44 stirrups 46.7 kg; 122.9 kg in all (side-face bars are listed the same way).
examples.check:
w=lambda p: p*p/162
import math
n=math.ceil((6000-100)/140+1)
b=4*6.54*w(20); t=2*6.54*w(12); s=n*1.72*w(10)
print(round(w(20),3),round(b,1),round(t,1),n,round(s,1),round(b+t+s,1))

traps: Measuring the nominal cover to the main bar. It is measured to the outermost steel, the stirrup; the main bar cover is 30 + 10 = 40 mm here.
Forgetting the stirrup diameter in the clear-spacing formula: subtract 2c and 2φ<sub>s</sub> before dividing by n − 1.
Taking 15 mm as the gap between two layers of 20 mm bars. The gap is the greatest of 15 mm, two thirds of the aggregate size and the bar diameter: 20 mm here.
Hooking a torsion stirrup at 90°. Use 135° hooks with 6φ extension, round a corner bar.
Using φ²/162 with φ in cm or getting kg instead of kg/m: a 16 mm bar weighs 1.58 kg per metre.

quiz.q: Define nominal cover and give its value for moderate exposure.
quiz.a: The design depth of concrete cover over all steel including links, shown on the drawing; 30 mm for moderate exposure.

quiz.q: State the minimum horizontal clear distance between bars.
quiz.a: The greater of the larger bar diameter and the nominal maximum aggregate size plus 5 mm.

quiz.q: Why does IS 456 set a maximum spacing for tension bars?
quiz.a: Widely spaced bars let flexural cracks open wide between them. Limiting the clear spacing (180 mm for Fe415) keeps crack widths acceptable at service loads.

quiz.q: A 250 mm wide beam has three 20 mm bars, 8 mm stirrups and 25 mm nominal cover. Find the clear spacing and check it.
quiz.a: Inside width = 250 − 50 − 16 = 184 mm. Clear spacing = (184 − 60)/2 = 62 mm. Minimum 25 mm, maximum 180 mm, so it is acceptable.

quiz.q: Find the weight of twelve 16 mm bars each 5.2 m long.
Find d for a 450 mm deep beam with 25 mm cover, 8 mm stirrups and one layer of 16 mm bars.
On site the stirrups are made 10 mm smaller all round than drawn. Which checks change and how?
quiz.a: The cover to the stirrups grows by 10 mm and the main bars move inward, so d falls by about 10 mm and the moment and shear capacities drop. The clear spacing between the bottom bars shrinks by 20/(n − 1) mm and may fall below the minimum. The stirrup no longer matches the schedule. The cage should be remade to the drawing.

quiz.q: Why are torsion stirrups hooked at 135° rather than 90°?
quiz.a: Torsion cracks spiral round all faces and the cover can spall at the corners. A 90° hook lies in the cover and opens when the cover goes; a 135° hook is bent back into the core round the corner bar, so the hoop stays closed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Detailing is now done in BIM models whose bar data goes straight to automatic bending machines, and clash checks catch bars that cannot fit at beam-column joints before they reach site. Earthquake codes (IS 13920) add closely spaced hoops near joints and stricter hooks. Stainless and epoxy-coated bars are used where cover alone cannot stop corrosion. Search for 'BIM reinforcement detailing', 'IS 13920 ductile detailing' and 'bar bending schedule software'.
